When it is said that a final cause is a cause by its essence of what causes the thing to exist, this does not mean that its essence, considered on its own, is a cause. It causes through its existence in the mind. — س ره
For the two matters; and it was for the two matters. — خ

The point seems to be that a group’s existence adds nothing to the existence of its members. For that reason, its being caused is no different from the members’ being caused. The group would then need a first cause, just as its members do. But some writers describe the group as having an existence added to the existence of its members. On that account, the group’s cause would be its members, each caused by the one before it, and there would be no need for a separate first cause of the group. This would undermine the proof. Even so, we can still question whether an endless group forms a whole in the same way as a finite group. — ط مده
For example, the links of a chain. But that example concerns finite lengths and dimensions.

The reply tries to make the objection seem like a denial of an obvious truth, so that it can be dismissed as stubbornness. But the shorter series need not fall behind only at its final end; it might fall behind at infinitely many points, while the longer one gains infinitely many members. The sound reply is narrower: the proof assumes that one series has a finite number of extra members. That cannot be denied. The first reply works only if linked lengths and connected causes cannot break off in the middle, and if the mind can grasp the full order at once. — س ره
One could challenge the claim that this is self-evident, and deny that equality or difference in size applies to endless quantities. — ط مده
This is especially so for those who say that multiplicity is only an idea, as do some who hold that existence and what exists are one. On their view, numbers are only levels of multiplicity. — س ره

The point is that only a finite number of counted things exists, and the numbers we derive from them are finite too. But the same reasoning would apply to the motions of the heavenly spheres, since only finitely many of those exist at one time. — س ره

The word “some” may be out of place here: all philosophers say that souls are without end, since the flow of existence never stops. In their books on logic, they use the rational soul as an example of a general kind with endless individual members. The souls’ endlessness is simultaneous, not successive. Otherwise, it would not be limited to human souls, since every kind—human beings, horses, cattle, and all other earthly kinds—has endless individual members over time. One answer is that the author is contrasting this view with that of those who say that souls become one after leaving their bodies. They compare this to water in many jars: when the jars break, the water joins together. — س ره

Al-Kubasāt objects that the matching proof cannot be trusted. Two endless series may differ in a way that concerns their finite limit, not the respect in which they are endless. For example, an endless series of hundreds and an endless series of thousands both go on forever, but their members differ in size. Matching their ends in imagination does not move the whole difference out of the finite part and into the endless part. As the mind keeps matching them, the extra amount shifts from the end toward the middle and keeps moving; it never reaches one fixed point or the last member. When the mind stops, the difference remains at the point where it stopped. In short, the difference never moves into the endless part. It always remains at a finite point, either at the end or somewhere in the middle. So, he says, hold to the argument and do not be confused. — ه ره

This is because the levels of number do not all exist, unlike the motions of the heavenly spheres. The point is not that numbers are only ideas, as in the theologians’ view. Many philosophers hold that numbers are real, separate quantities. — س ره

This is the strongest argument, because the whole series has no existence beyond the individual events, as the author will show. So this does not apply a claim about each member to a separate whole. The whole is nothing but the events, each of which is finite; it is not one event that is itself finite. The same applies to a general kind, which exists only through its individual members. The supposed beginninglessness and permanence of a general kind come from confusing what exists in the mind with what exists outside it. — س ره

If the two series cannot be equal, how could one be greater? “Equal” here means equal in their pattern of growth. Al-Tusi’s point is that after matching, the series that starts one year ago must be equal to, greater than, or smaller than the one that starts now. The first two options are impossible, so the third follows—and that means the two series are finite. — س ره

Do not think this argument simply changes the proof. It does bring in the argument from reciprocal relations, but that argument counts paired things; it does not need an order or two series, which the matching argument does need. The author makes the work easier by saying that the two series already match in reality, without asking us to imagine a match. On the disputed side, the earlier events must then outnumber the later ones, because their counts must balance. The two series are like two lines that agree at every point except their ends, so both must have ends. The series are taken as what gives rise to these relations and makes them real.

The claim that an earlier event at one end has a later event at the other end that is not itself earlier depends only on how we look at them. In reality, whatever event we choose as the latest is also earlier than what follows it. This is especially clear in time and motion, which have no first or last part. The same is true of a continuous line: no later part fails to be earlier than another part. So the argument does not apply to the motions of the heavenly spheres or to time as a continuous length. It differs from a chain of causes and effects, where there is a final effect that needs a cause, whose cause needs another cause, and so on without end. There, the number of earlier and later causes and effects must balance, so the argument requires them to be finite. Also, events that occur one after another do not all exist at the same time; only one exists at any moment. So they do not form an actual series that can be matched. The author presents the argument in a way that fits the theologians’ view. — س ره

This depends on the series stopping in the future, so that there would be a later event that is not earlier than anything else. That would make the later events in the past more numerous than the earlier ones. But why could the series not be impossible to stop, and so continue forever into the future? Then the earlier and later events in the series would be equal. — ط مده

If number is only an idea, then only the things we count really exist. The ordered numbers themselves do not. What actually exists has no order of number built into it. For example, which of the separate souls that exist together from eternity is the one counted as three, and which as four? There is no reason to choose one rather than another. So how could this order apply to them? This is really a point against the claim that each number is made up of the numbers below it. — س ره

The author does not use an argument some people offer: that a group of people captured a city, though no one person captured it alone. That proves only that the group differs from each person; it does not prove that the group has a separate existence. The group might be an idea drawn from its members, as fatherhood is drawn from Zayd and his child. The later example of several people moving a heavy stone will make this clearer. — س ره
“The whole” here means the whole in relation to what lies outside it. A whole ends when all its parts end, just as it ends when any one part ends. — س ره

When people say that a whole has an existence beyond that of each individual part, they mean the members taken together as a whole. They do not mean one thing made up of the members plus the description “together.” The fact that many things are arranged as one is a separate description of them. Or they mean the whole under the condition that its parts are arranged together. They do not mean that the arrangement itself is one of the parts: that arrangement is only an idea, or it would itself need another arrangement, and so on forever. — س ره

On this view, the whole exists, even if it exists only through the same existence as its individual members. This is like existence and essence, or broader kind and difference, in simple things. A chain of causes and effects is a whole of this kind; on their view, it still needs a separate cause. — س ره

In fact, the opposite was established. The members taken together come first as causes, while the whole under the condition that they are arranged together comes later as an effect. The details are discussed in Shawāriq by the scholar Lāhījī. — س ره

One might object that all the infinitely many chains taken together also form a whole that exists in its own right and must have a cause. Is that cause the whole itself, one of its parts, or something outside it? The author will address this shortly by defining the whole as all existing possible things. — س ره
For example, some hold that there are infinitely many motions, times, and souls, all of which depend on the Necessary Being. — س ره

Some also use this objection to argue that a thing can cause itself; the objection and answer are much alike. The argument works only if the whole has an existence beyond the existence of its members, which the author will deny. I would add that if the Necessary Being and all possible things formed one independently existing whole, the Necessary Being would be part of something else. Yet the Necessary Being has no parts and cannot be a part of another thing; that would also make God limited. God has no equal, rival, or second, and encompasses all things. If by this “whole” we mean only the concepts of the Necessary Being and the natures of possible things, then it plainly does not exist as a real thing. The concept “Necessary Being” is necessary only by definition; as something in the mind, it is possible. Have they not heard that God’s unity is absolute, not numerical; that God is not one item among other existing things, and is not detached from them? In any case, even setting aside these points, their own books state that the Necessary Being is not part of anything else. Yet on their view, this proposed composite would exist as a distinct thing. — س ره

The remaining parts would then depend on this cause, directly or through other causes. This is the least degree of independence, since the remaining parts depend on it through intermediaries. The greatest degree is when they all depend on it directly. — س ره

This objection applies to the premise only if it is taken as a universal rule. In the case under discussion, all the parts of the chain exist together, since the argument concerns a chain of causes and effects that exists all at once. But the author may be giving an example of a later effect taking the place of an earlier cause in the order of rank—for instance, the tenth intellect taking the rank of the first intellect in relation to the Necessary Being—or of an effect lagging behind its cause. — س ره
Rank is considered only from the end where the series has a limit; from the other side, only causal order is considered, because there is no fixed beginning there. — س ره

This feature belongs on the side of the effect, not the cause. In the same way, possibility and whatever else the first effect depends on are considered on the effect’s side; they do not compromise the simplicity of its complete cause. Also, the discussion here concerns the independence of an efficient cause, while the final effect is considered on the side of the material cause. — س ره
This reply changes the argument instead of answering it, which is not proper in a debate. — س ره
This is the point made when the original proof was stated, as explained earlier. — س ره

A condition may be necessary for something to exist: if the condition is absent, the thing is absent too. But the thing does not necessarily exist whenever the condition is present. The same is true of an incomplete cause. A complete cause, however, does produce its effect. — س ره

One might object: if the whole depends on each individual part, then its cause is the individuals taken together, not the whole itself. That would avoid saying that something causes itself. Besides, no single individual part is a complete cause. We reply that saying the whole depends on each part does not mean that each part is its complete cause. On this view, the whole itself is the complete cause. The point is that it does not depend on a complete cause outside itself. It is enough that an effect depends on every part of its complete cause and on that cause coming before it. In this view, “what an effect depends on” describes causes short of the complete cause. — س ره

Examples include a thing causing its own cause, as in a causal circle, or depending on itself. This does not mean that it is its own condition or one of its own parts; those would amount to saying that it causes itself. — س ره
The group exists only in the mind. — س ره

They may say that each whole is another existent, but they do not mean that it is a third, single thing counted as one. With a walnut and an almond, for example, the whole is not a third item beside the walnut and the almond, like a pistachio would be. Nor is it a separate arrangement that exists on its own. Instead, it is an existent that is both walnut and almond: one existent is only the walnut, another is only the almond, and a third is the walnut and almond together. This third is “another” because the walnut alone is one, the almond alone is another, and their whole is many things with parts, not one thing.

This differs from the author’s view. He says that a whole is not a separate existent, because it is many, and existence goes with unity. These thinkers do not accept that existence must mean unity. As Avicenna says, many things can exist as many, even though they are not one. On their view, the repeated parts are clear: if the walnut-and-almond whole is a third thing, as the critic claims, and its arrangement exists only in the mind, then the walnut and almond are repeated inside the three-part whole. They say that number exists in its own right in this sense. The author says that number exists through what the mind draws it from: the units that make it up. Here, “all the units together” means each individual unit; the proponents of a separate whole use the phrase in the way just described.

One might ask why the author raises the problem of an endless chain at every division, as before. The answer is that his objection is a proof, not just a way of forcing an opponent to accept a consequence. If the two sides of a division were a separate existent and existence necessarily meant unity, there would be another one beyond them. But these thinkers do not accept that existence must mean unity. For them, existence is broader, so the whole can exist as many. A general kind, for example, exists through its many instances. It is distinct from its particular features through its generality, not through another special feature. This point has been explained at length because it is subtle. — س ره

The earlier discussion of unity and multiplicity allows us to say both that each number is simply its units taken together and that it is more than that, since “units taken together” is a general kind shared by every number. That apparent difference may be only in how the mind arranges the units. In the outside world, numbers are just fewer or more units. — س ره

Both ways of putting the argument can be challenged by denying that an effect can exist without itself causing something further. This objection applies whether the chain is made up of complete causes or incomplete ones. In other words, one can deny that the chain stops at the end where future effects would follow. — ط مده

Sayyid Dāmād did well in Qabasāt not to rely on intuition alone. He gave this rule: if a general judgment applies to every individual in every way that individual can exist—either on its own or considered together with others—then it also applies to the whole. But if the judgment applies to each individual only when it is separate from the others, the whole may have a different judgment. For example, “possible” applies to every possible thing, and “changing” applies to every natural event. Those judgments also apply to the whole. But one loaf may be enough to satisfy each person individually; that does not mean it is enough for a whole group. — س ره

The group whose size matches the number of thousand-groups may not lie neatly at the finite end or the infinite end. It may be woven through the other group, with no clear point where the second group begins. Also, choosing units so that one group has a certain multiple of the other has no basis outside the mind. — س ره

Think of bricks leaning on one another, or bodies resting on one another. Unless something supports them, there are no leaning bricks or supported bodies. Remove one, and all the ones after it fall because of the order of dependence between them. — س ره

Here, infinitely many possible things are treated like one possible thing: two equally possible options do not become actual unless something outside them makes one take precedence, and either may fail to exist. Only a necessary cause can remove every way an effect might fail to exist; a possible cause cannot. So the chain cannot enter reality if each member’s existence depends on a condition that has not itself been made actual. — س ره

There is another way to argue against an endless chain. We have established that bringing things into existence and causing things belong to existence itself. A caused thing does not exist on its own; its existence depends on its cause. The self-standing existence that supports it is the existence of its cause. If the chain went on without end, there would be dependent existences linked to one another, with no independent existence to support them. That is impossible. This link between cause and effect is not just an idea in the mind, so it is not enough to say that each is independent of the other in some limited way. The link reflects real degrees of stronger and weaker existence. This argument also rules out a circle of causes. It resembles the eighth proof, but the two arguments use different starting points. — ط مده

The author limits this proof to things that exist together, so it does not apply to things that occur one after another: such things are not all distinct in the outside world at the same time, and their number in the mind is finite. I would add that the proof is challenged by things some thinkers regard as actually infinite: rational souls that have left their bodies, according to philosophers; forms in the imaginal world, according to Illuminationist thinkers; the particular names of God and their mental forms, called “fixed realities” by mystics; God’s words that never run out or perish; divine manifestations, the joys of the people of Paradise, and the punishments of the people of Hell, according to religious thinkers; mental forms in God’s essence, according to Anaximenes; fixed natures, according to the Muʿtazilites; and the horizontal intellects, if perfected souls join them after leaving their bodies, according to Illuminationist thinkers. As their master says in The Philosophy of Illumination, perfected souls that have left their bodies join the dominant lights, increasing the number of sacred lights without end.

This also gives the beginning of a proof for God’s oneness. If these actual infinities were truly many, they would form numbers. Numbers are even or odd, and either way the chain would have to be finite—contrary to the claim that it is infinite. So the multiplicity here cannot exist in reality. — س ره

The Sayyid’s clarification may have three meanings. First, he may mean that an infinite chain toward effects is impossible in itself, as shown by proofs that the downward flow of existence ends in a vertical order, even if it continues across different kinds. But the arguments used against an infinite chain of causes—comparison, reciprocal relations, and different causal roles—would not apply to it. Second, he may mean that such a chain is possible in itself but has not occurred. Third, he may mean that it is possible in reality, which cannot be the point: if it were, the chain of simple beings would not end in basic matter, nor would the higher worlds end in the world of nature. Illuminationist philosophers say that the highest lights descend to a highest light that produces no further light below it, much as physical light reaches a point where it produces no further light because of distance and obstructions. Philosophers in Aristotle’s school say that the intellects end with the tenth intellect. The first interpretation also seems unlikely, because the proof establishes that the chain of simple substances ends; it does not show that a thing cannot have an essential property, which in turn has another essential property, without end. At most, such a chain has not occurred. The second interpretation therefore remains. — س ره

That is, the real cause and the means through which an effect exists. The proofs are the means of establishing that the chain is impossible. So there is no contradiction between saying that the chain does not exist in reality and assuming it for arguments such as one-to-one comparison. Those arguments begin by considering the possibility of infinitely many causes, each existing with its effect. — س ره
Just as a cause exists at its own level, which is prior to the effect, it also exists at the level of the effect itself. — س ره

The distinction is valid, but it does not prevent the proofs from applying to a descending chain of effects. We are discussing real causes, not causes that merely prepare the way for an effect. When a real cause that necessitates its effects exists, all those effects exist with it, since a true effect cannot be delayed beyond its true cause. Each thing may exist at its own level, but if those levels do not form a real ordered series of existence, then there is no chain in either direction. In that case, one-to-one comparison and the other proofs apply, because the individual things exist together when their causes do. I wonder why the author has said neither yes nor no. Perhaps he remained silent out of deference. God knows best what his servants mean. — س ره

An effect has no feature that is not also present in its cause, but the cause has features that the effect does not. What has been shown so far is that the effects in a descending chain do not all exist together; it has not been shown that they are not ordered, unless the author's point is that the proofs require both features at once. — س ره
This conclusion follows from everything said earlier, not only from the claim that form also counts as an efficient cause. That is why the author can speak of all the levels of causes. — س ره

In other words, matter can mean either what receives a form or what bears the potential for the thing whose matter it is. “Receiver” and “matter” can also refer either to what exists together with a form or to what exists before that form is present. — س ره

One might object that this assumes what it is trying to prove: the question is whether the parts of an essence—its matter and form—can be infinite. The reply is that this is not circular. The parts at issue in the conclusion are parts of the essence understood by the mind. Their being finite is already established, since otherwise the essence could not be understood, its definition could not be complete, and there could be no highest kind. — س ره

Neither kind of element, taken universally, needs matter in the sense of a bearer of potential; those general kinds are created directly. Only particular instances that arise in time need matter. There is no problem with an endless succession of material things here, because they occur one after another. — س ره

This proves that an endless chain is impossible only as it rises from what is less complete to what is more complete. It does not prove that an endless chain is impossible as it descends from the more complete to what came before it, as the previous clarification explained. — ط مده

By defining matter as the subject that bears a thing's possibility, the author makes clear that this division concerns matter that bears potential and comes before a thing in time, not prime matter, which receives form and is prior to it by nature. Otherwise, the claim that a new quality does not remove anything would not apply: prime matter receives a form that was not there before. The definition also rules out matter considered without any form at all. — س ره

This does not apply to successive levels of development that do not work by replacing one form with another. In these cases, matter takes on one form and then another; the plant and animal forms, for example, are substantial forms, not accidents. The deeper answer is that there are not several forms here, as discussed in the Journey of the Soul, but one form that grows stronger and moves from incompleteness toward perfection. — س ره
This is equivalent to saying, “or if it does not remain.” — س ره

A false belief, considered as a mental image and state of the soul, can perfect the soul, even though it fails to match the outside world. Its being harmful is a relative matter. This applies to blameworthy qualities too. The point follows from the view that evil is relative: nothing is evil in itself simply because it exists. — ط مده
The Arabic leaves out an implied word: “the judgment that change can be reversed applies only to this kind.” — س ره
Elemental forms remain present in compound things. — س ره

This is true if we imagine one simple element moving toward something opposed to it. But if it combines with another element that is active against it, and their powers are moderated, a balanced mixture arises. The mixture is not opposed to what it becomes. That is how things stand with compound kinds, so the claim in the main text can be challenged. — ط مده

Just as thinkers say that a mixture has a balanced quality after the elements have acted on one another—cooler than pure heat, warmer than pure cold, and so on—we say that, alongside the pure forms of the elements, the mixture has an intermediate substantial form. It is earth in relation to pure water and water in relation to pure earth, and likewise for the other elements. Just as pure earth is earth, this intermediate form is a degree of earth; the difference is one of greater or lesser intensity. The same is true of water, air, and fire. From this, the commentator draws the idea of substantial motion: substance itself can grow stronger or weaker. This account reconciles the view that the elemental forms remain with the view that they are shed: their pure, fully distinct forms do not remain, but their intermediate forms, unified in the mixture, do. That is why this is called an Eastern wisdom. — س ره

The feature must be something that also describes the active thing, as evenness describes the number four. This rules out an action that is not a feature of what it acts on, and a feature that is not an action, such as God's true attributes. A thing's being described by something is not always the same as receiving it. In the passive sense, receiving means that an outside cause gives a feature to a thing through matter, as water receives heat. Fire's being hot by nature is different. — س ره

If acting and receiving are both effects produced by an active and a receptive cause, this would make the receptive cause a kind of active cause, against the distinctions established earlier. If “effect” means only that a feature belongs to something, the argument against many effects from one simple cause does not apply. That argument uses “effect” in its proper sense of something caused by an agent. — ط مده

The claim is that existence exists in itself, unity is one in itself, and causing causes in itself. But if causing were a real feature, it would be something possible and would need a cause. Saying that it causes by its own nature does not remove that need, just as saying that an event begins by itself would not explain how it came to exist. — س ره

The speaker uses a noun where a pronoun is expected: “what it produces” instead of “what is produced by it.” The commentator finds this surprising, since being affected is itself a kind of receptivity. — س ره

This is even more surprising than the previous point. The fact that two ideas have different meanings does not explain why both are true of the thing being described. What matters is whether the thing itself has different aspects that make both descriptions true. An intellect can know itself without needing two separate aspects, but a thing that moves and is moved must differ in the relevant way. The same applies to claims about God's knowledge, power, life, and will: the truth of all these descriptions cannot be explained by saying that the concepts differ, since all of them describe the same single divine reality. — س ره
Even if this were granted, the thing would not be simple: it would act by virtue of its existence and receive by virtue of its essence. — س ره

It would be clearer to replace “necessity and possibility” with “actuality and potentiality.” A recipient has its effect only as a possibility: it lacks what it may receive. An active cause has its effect in actuality: it has the perfection it gives. If the source and recipient were one, the thing would both have and lack the same effect, which is impossible. Strictly speaking, necessity applies to a complete cause, not to every one of the four kinds of cause by itself. It applies directly to a cause whose only cause is the agent, such as an immaterial effect that follows from its own possibility and the active cause that is also its goal. — ط مده

As explained earlier, possibility in itself is a kind of lack, so it is not a necessary feature in the strict sense. There is no active and passive relation here unless “possibility” means that either of two outcomes remains open. — س ره
If these abstract attributes are only ideas in the mind, they do not need to be made or caused, just as the ideas of acting and being affected do not. — س ره

This is not the only argument for the point. The unity of God's real attributes with His essence is one of the best-known proofs among philosophers, as in The Beginning and the Return and other works. — س ره

The cause of bodies and their natures must be something separate from matter, not the powers, natural processes, or souls that work through matter. First, these can start natural movement but cannot give existence itself; only what is free from potentiality can give existence. Second, they are themselves in motion, and something in motion is between potentiality and actuality, so it cannot be the source of existence. Third, bodily powers affect things only through their position relative to matter. But the question here is what brings matter itself into existence, and position cannot relate an agent to something nonexistent or to prime matter. An immaterial cause is different in all these ways. — س ره
That is, the sources are thoughts or acts of knowing. This follows once we add that every immaterial thing is an intellect: it knows and can be known. — س ره
“Thought” here means a firm judgment, not a passing image. What tips the choice is the belief that the action serves some end. — س ره

This is close to the first example. In the second, the point is that thought gives rise to the will, or strong desire. In the first, thought makes one of two opposite actions more likely than the other. The fact that desire and resolve come between thought and movement does not matter: the argument is that no bodily tool intervenes. — س ره
There is room to challenge this example. We will return to it when discussing the six kinds of agent, God willing. — ط مد

If “general” has its usual meaning, the objection is clear. If it means that God's knowledge and will extend to everything, which seems to be what the author intends, the problem is that they relate equally to all particular things and do not by themselves single out a limited number of them. — س ره

This may mean a particular intellect, or intellect in general, depending on the view held by Aristotle’s followers that separate intellects do not directly know particular things outside themselves. — س ره

That is, its own possibility alone is enough. Although such a thing is particular because it cannot be shared by many, it is separate from matter, time, place, and the readiness of a material recipient. So eternal knowledge and will can grasp it. — س ره

In short, there is no problem with eternal will relating to things created without matter or brought into being directly. Nor is there a problem with its relating to things that begin in time, because the complete cause of every new event includes both an enduring first principle and a new condition. — س ره

The two motions are alike, though their subjects—the surface of the celestial sphere and the surface of fire—are different. Both can receive motion that is faster or slower. The commentator points to the rising and setting of comets and similar heavenly bodies. — س ره
The subjects differ in kind, even though the Sun and Moon are both celestial bodies. Each heavenly kind has only one individual. — س ره

Perhaps Avicenna bases his view on the claim that, for these philosophers, strength and weakness belong to qualities, while existence is neither a property belonging to something else nor a substance existing in its own right. But the author’s reading seems better, since Avicenna describes existence as stronger or weaker. His phrase “existence as existence” alone does not prove that he meant the mind’s general idea of existence. — س ره

Some thinkers deny that a complete cause comes before its effect because the cause’s matter and form are present with the compound effect and seem to be the effect itself. The reply is that matter and form are counted as parts of the cause, not as parts of the single effect. The effect considered on its own is one thing: the form that makes it what it is. So the matter and form in the compound do not make the cause and effect identical, as the objection assumes. Once the simple form exists, the compound made from it and its nearby matter follows at the same level, gathering in a higher way the perfections already present in the form. The compound exists as a by-product of the form and needs no new cause of its own. This explains how the complete cause comes before the effect in its own right, while existing alongside the compound that follows from it only as a by-product. The commentator says this also helps with the question of resurrection. He adds that there is no need to use al-Lāhījī’s different but reasonable answer: the cause comes first as all its parts taken together, while the effect comes after when those same parts are joined. — س ره

The form is free from having to carry out material, earthly actions, but not from the immaterial forms of those actions in the afterlife—such as a body made entirely of form, sensing, nourishment, and sexual union. These follow from it by nature, even though it does not need them, just as a mature plant no longer needs to grow. The reason is that a simple intellect contains, in a higher way, the realities of the lower powers. It directly knows what is seen, heard, and otherwise sensed, without sense organs, and acts with full power, without bodily movement-powers. This applies to the simple intellect; other cases differ, as noted earlier. — س ره

Philosophers agree that there are four kinds of cause. They argue for goals as causes in their discussion of ends, and for matter and form in their discussion of matter and form. They treat active causes as self-evident. Some natural scientists today build their work on the claim that matter is the only cause. They therefore accuse philosophers of believing in chance, since philosophers say that the world depends on an agent without matter—God. The commentator says the philosophers are right. When physical things interact, their active and receptive effects differ. If fire ignites cotton, the fire contributes one effect and the cotton another. Fire’s effect is already present in it and passes to the cotton, though not like a liquid being poured out. The cotton’s effect is not present before the two meet; it receives that effect from the fire. This is how physical events work in general. Matter can therefore be seen in two ways: as something that has an effect and gives it to something else, or as something that lacks the effect and receives it. The first is an active cause; the second is a receptive cause. — ط مده

This kind of cause is called luck or chance. It occurs in the world of physical things, not in the universal order of creation. Luck and chance apply only when we look at a small part of the order, not at the whole order of the universe. — ن ره
Here matter means the bearer of a thing’s potential, as explained earlier. — ن ره

This applies to voluntary actions, which depend on a prior thought that includes belief in a goal. The author calls this a goal in a loose sense. Strictly speaking, a goal is the perfection an action reaches or the perfection the agent wants, and for which the action is done. — ط مده

The careful thinker seems to mean by “simple” that the thing is not made of distinct mental parts such as matter and form. On this reading, his argument has a problem: philosophers agree that accidents are simple in the outside world, and each kind of thing causes the accidents that belong to it. That cause would either be simple, which would make the kind eternal, or compound, which would mean that a simple accident comes from a compound cause. But the author later says that the soul is not simple. This suggests that he uses “simple” to mean “not made of distinct parts that exist”—whether those parts are in the mind or outside it. On that reading, the objection from accidents fails, because accidents depend on a subject for their existence, just as the soul depends on the body. A further problem remains: the parts and combinations of things that arise in nature must eventually end in simple things. Otherwise, the chain of parts would never reach anything that could exist, and new things would be made from eternal matter and forms—an impossible result. The author later answers that the coming into being of the formal part is built into its nature, so it needs no cause. But if this depends on the view that substance itself is in motion, it does not prove either that the cause of a new thing is compound or that every new thing is compound. — ط مده

The compound cause is made in thought from two parts: one lasting part, the unchanging face of God that shines on every matter ready to receive it—or the separate intellect that lasts through God’s lasting, one of His active names and attributes, such as the Tenth Intellect that brings about compounds in this world—and one new part, a portion of the turning motion of the heavenly sphere. — س ره

The commentator suggests a better reply: a part of a newly formed thing is not a separate new thing that needs its own separate cause; the cause of the whole compound is enough. The author’s claim that coming into being is built into the part’s nature, and so needs no cause, works only if “coming into being” means continuous self-renewal. It does not work if it means beginning to exist after not existing. A part of a new thing comes into being in that second sense too, so something must determine that it begins to exist. That cause also begins to exist, and so on without end. — س ره

That is, motion like a change in place. The motion of nature is also a kind of motion, but it is motion in substance itself. The two accounts agree, except that the first locates the conditions for coming into being in portions of the heavenly sphere’s changing position, while the author locates them in portions of the continuously flowing celestial nature that keeps time. Other natures do not continue in this way. — س ره

This is the Illuminationist Shaykh, who discusses the argument in his book The Wisdom of Illumination. For him, each whole exists as a unity over and above its individual parts. He therefore allows some intellects to come from a group of other intellects, and some to come from a whole made up of two aspects, such as two features within the intellects. His view will be explained later. The cause of every affected being has a real unity. One might object that if the simple effect begins to exist after not existing, and if, as already stated, a simple new thing cannot come from a compound, this would lead to an endless chain. The reply is that the Active Intellect is its active cause, the source from which it receives existence: it is one and simple, but it acts under an outside condition, namely a portion of the heavenly motion. The Shaykh’s point is that the active cause cannot itself be compound, a whole made up of two or more things. He says the whole is the cause, not each part on its own, even though the coming together of the parts does not itself exist as a thing. The complete cause of a new event, however, may be compound—for example, something lasting together with a new condition. Other philosophers say the complete cause of a new event is a group of conditions, some of which are absences, such as removing an obstacle or preparing matter. The author has also cited the writer of The Mawāqif, who treats removing an obstacle as the presence of something. A true unity in the world of events, though simple in one respect, may also be compound in another, as the author will explain. — س ره

The commentator groups the chapter’s claims this way: a possible thing must exist when its complete cause is present and cannot exist when that cause is absent; without either condition, it remains possible in itself. A cause need not coincide in time with the effect’s earlier nonexistence. Coming into being after nonexistence is part of the nature of what comes into being, just as possibility is part of an essence. These features are not separately made by the agent. Nor does being new explain why a thing needs a cause; what makes something need a cause must itself be dependent in its own nature. — س ره
In other words, matter serves as an intermediary through its readiness to receive a form, and this role of matter explains why the result begins in time. — ن ره
